title: Animal models of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.
text_summary: 本文综述非酒精性脂肪性肝病的动物模型，并以人类NAFLD/NASH的脂肪变、气球样变、炎症和纤维化为参照。文章比较蛋氨酸胆碱缺乏、高脂、高蔗糖/果糖、胆固醇等饮食模型，以及ob/ob、db/db、炎症信号和免疫相关基因模型。不同模型可重现脂肪堆积、胰岛素抵抗、炎症或纤维化中的部分环节，但很少完整模拟人类疾病的代谢背景和自然进展。作者强调应按研究问题选择模型，并通过结合饮食、遗传和炎症因素提高转化相关性。

Animal models of nonalcoholic fatty
liver disease
Lionel Hebbard and Jacob George
Abstract | In 1980, Ludwig and colleagues described a series of patients with liver histology characterized
by the accumulation of fat and the presence of hepatic necroinflammation in the absence of a history of
excessive alcohol consumption. They coined the term nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), which today
is regarded as one of the most common causes of liver disease in affluent countries. NASH is a subset
of a larger spectrum of diseases termed fatty liver disease (including alcoholic and nonalcoholic fatty liver
disease; AFLD and NAFLD, respectively). NAFLD and NASH are linked to visceral adiposity, insulin resistance,
dyslipidemia and type 2 diabetes, and are increasing due to the prevalence of the metabolic syndrome. In this
context, research has been undertaken using animals to model human steatosis and NAFLD to NASH disease
progression. This Review discusses the prevalent dietary and inflammation-based genetic animal models
described in recent years.
Hebbard, L. & George, J. Nat. Rev. Gastroenterol. Hepatol. 8, 34–44 (2011); published online 30 November 2010; doi:10.1038/nrgastro.2010.191

Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a con­
tinuum of diseases that includes simple steatosis (non­
alcoholic fatty liver) and steatohepatitis (nonalcoholic
steatohepatitis; NASH) that develops in the absence of
excessive alcohol intake. NAFLD and NASH ultimately
lead to the development of cirrhosis and hepatocellular
carcinoma (HCC).1 Since the initial description of NASH
by Ludwig et al. in 1980,2 multiple studies have defined
the following clinical features to be associated with the
development of NAFLD and NASH: overweight and
obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, hypertension
and dyslipidemia. Furthermore, given the growing
number of individuals who are overweight or obese in
the USA (currently >60%3), NAFLD may account for a
third of future HCC cases in this country.4
Of importance, overweight and obesity is now regarded
as a chronic, low­grade, inflammatory condition with
activation of the innate immune system and infiltration
of adipose tissue by activated macrophages. In turn, the
inflamed adipose tissue can drive liver disease. Population
studies now link obesity, the metabolic syndrome and
viral hepatitis to an increase in the relative risk of HCC
up to 265­fold for obese patients with HBV infection and
135­fold for obese patients with HCV infection, indicat­
ing the synergistic detrimental effects of obesity on viral
hepatitis.5 Thus, given the links between overweight
and obesity and NAFLD and NASH, and the emerging
association with HCC, a major and growing public health
problem is rapidly developing in many countries.
To understand more fully the process of fatty liver
formation, numerous cross­sectional clinical studies

have been undertaken. However, NAFLD and/or NASH
can take decades to evolve and progress, which limits the
quality of longitudinal data. Furthermore, the ethical con­
straints on obtaining human liver tissue limit the interpret­
ability of the data. Hence, researchers have turned their
attention to the development of suitable animal models
to test the role of molecules and molecular pathways
in fatty liver formation. These models offer the oppor­
tunity to take a reductionist approach to assess the role
of a gene or dietary factor—or a combination of
the two—to the disease process. This Review discusses the
benchmark animal models that recapitulate the pathology
and metabolic dysfunction associated with NALFD. To
start, we will broadly introduce the histology of human
fatty liver as a point of reference for animal models.

Histology of NAFLD

The hallmark of NAFLD is steatosis—the accumulation
of intracytoplasmic lipid as triglycerides within hepato­
cytes. In the clinic, noninvasive tests aid in the diagnosis
of NAFLD.6 However, liver biopsy and subsequent histol­
ogy is the gold standard for confirming the presence and
activity of the disease.7 The grading and staging systems
for NAFLD as it transitions from simple steatosis to
NASH have been developed by Brunt and colleagues8
and the NASH Clinical Research Network. 9 These
systems consider the extent of steatosis, hepatocellular
injury, inflammation and fibrosis. The size of the lipid
vacuoles can differ; macrovesicular steatosis is character­
ized by large vacuoles that occupy the whole cytoplasm.
Macrovesicular steatosis typically pushes the nucleus to
one side of the cell and is the predominant pattern seen in
NAFLD and alcoholic liver disease.10 However, in some
instances the cytoplasm contains multiple small lipid

vacuoles and the nucleus is unmoved; this is described
as microvesicular steatosis.11 Patients can present with
both forms.
In contrast to simple steatosis, steatohepatitis (NASH) is
characterized by inflammation with the presence of steato­
sis, hepatocellular ballooning and both lobular and portal
inflammation with or without the presence of Mallory
bodies and fibrosis. Hepatocellular ballooning refers to
cells with swollen and rarefied cytoplasm, and has been
suggested to be an important distinguishing feature of
progressive disease compared with NAFLD.12 Ballooning
is often associated with Mallory’s hyaline, which is the
result of the clumping of cytokeratins and subsequent
ubiquitination.13 Lobular inflammation is characterized
by the presence of small clusters of inflammatory cells,
including lymphocytes, eosinophils and neutrophils,
near ballooned hepatocytes;7 it reflects dysregulation
of cytokine and chemokine expression in the fatty liver.
Finally, the presence of fibrosis is significant as it sug­
gests progression of liver disease (Figure 1). Pericellular
fibrosis typically has a chicken­wire pattern with collagen
secreted from hepatic stellate cells surrounding individual
or groups of hepatocytes. with centrilobular hepatocyte
replicative arrest, fibrosis can spread to the portal area
and subsequently lead to portal–portal and portal–central
bridging fibrosis and cirrhosis.8
examples of normal human liver, NAFLD and NASH
pathology are shown in Figure 1. For further reading,
two recent reviews examine in detail the pathology of
NAFLD7,14 and a position statement from the european
Association for the Study of the Liver proposes diag­
nostic criteria for classifying the disease.15 In the context
of the aforementioned information, the primary goal of
animal models of NAFLD is to replicate the pathogenesis
process in vivo and this is verified by the readout of
representative histology.

Pathogenesis of NAFLD

The development and progression of NAFLD to NASH
represents a complex pathophysiological process. The
traditional model for the development of steatohepatitis
is the ‘two­hit’ model. The first hit is the development
of a fatty liver in the context of obesity and consequent
peripheral and hepatic insulin resistance. The second step
encompasses the interplay of injury processes—including
a

b

Key points
■ Hepatic steatosis is associated with the metabolic syndrome
■ No dietary animal model can fully recapitulate the human steatosis disease
process
■ Genetic models have shown adipose inflammation to drive hepatic steatosis
■ Cholesterol promotes hepatic inflammation

oxidative stress, cytokine­mediated liver injury, altered
lipid partitioning and hepato toxicity mediated by
free fatty acids, abnormal intrahepatic chole sterol
loading, hyperinsulinemia, hyperleptinemia, hypo­
adiponectinemia and apoptosis—which lead to necro­
inflammation and ultimately fibrosis.16,17 Although this
scheme represents a useful model for progression of
NAFLD, data from animal models have shown that the
secondary hits per se can induce fatty liver formation.
For example, steatosis can result from increased lipid­
peroxidation­associated oxidative stress,18 TNF expres­
sion stimulated by free fatty acids,19 and inflammation
generated by adipocyte­specific Fas. 20 These studies
suggest that fatty liver formation and inflammation
(steatohepatitis) often develop simultaneously through
multiple inter­related hits. we, therefore, suggest that
a more appropriate term and model reflecting current
knowledge of NAFLD pathogenesis is the ‘integrated
response’ model (Figure 2).
To date, no single animal model has encompassed the
full spectrum of human disease progression, but they
can imitate particular characteristics of human disease.
Therefore, it is important that the researcher choose the
appropriate animal model to best answer their research
question. In the following section we present the major
animal models and describe their principle mechanism
for driving fatty liver formation.

Dietary-based animal models
rodent models
Methionine and choline deficiency
The primary driver of NAFLD is overnutrition and a
sedentary lifestyle leading to increased weight and, ulti­
mately, obesity. The majority of animal models focus
on providing a diet that cause liver damage. The model
used most often is actually nutrient deficient (Table 1).
The methionine and choline deficient (MCD) diet is

high in sucrose and fat (40% sucrose, 10% fat), but lacks
methionine and choline, which are essential for hepatic
β­oxidation and the production of very low density lipo­
protein (VLDL).21 This results in the accumulation of
intrahepatic lipid and decreased VLDL synthesis.
Rats and mice fed the MCD diet lose weight (up to
40% in 10 weeks). with a loss of white adipose tissue,
the liver decreases proportionally in size, develops
prominent steatosis in zone 3 (pericentral) and subse­
quent necroinflammation. The chicken­wire fibrosis that
develops resembles that seen in human NASH.22–27 The
severity of NASH that develops in mice fed the MCD
diet depends on rodent gender and strain.28 MCD­fed
mice exhibit increased inflammation by way of acti­
vated macrophage infiltration into the liver, the activa­
tion of nuclear factor κB (NFκB) and concomitant
increases in interleukin 6 (IL­6), transforming growth
factor β (TGF­β) and tumor necrosis factor (TNF).29–32
Furthermore, the MCD diet promotes increased expres­
sion of intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM1),
vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM1) and macro­
phage chemotactic protein 1 (MCP1) consistent with
raised macrophage phagocytic activity and increased
leukocyte adherence.30,31,33

Although the MCD diet promotes liver damage—as
confirmed by increased serum alanine aminotransferase
(ALT) levels—there are parallel reductions in plasma
triglyceride and cholesterol levels that go against those
seen in overweight and obese individuals with fatty
liver disease.24–27 Moreover, a major disadvantage of the
MCD diet is that the metabolic profile is opposite to that
seen in patients, namely, that insulin, leptin and glucose
levels are reduced, serum adiponectin is not reduced
and the animals are peripherally insulin sensitive.34–36
Nevertheless, studies have shown that the MCD diet
does reduce hepatic insulin sensitivity through the action
of oxidative stress and c­Jun N­terminal kinase (JNK)
activation to suppress insulin receptor activity.37,38
The choline­deficient, l­amino acid defined (CDAA)
diet has also been used as a rodent model of steatosis.39,40
Like the MCD diet, it inhibits fatty acid oxidation in
hepatocytes and NASH can result, but this requires a
longer time frame. wild­type mice on the CDAA diet
do not gain weight or have changes in peripheral insulin
sensitivity.41 Thus, the MCD and CDAA diets can be
used to probe changes in liver injury, regeneration and
pathways involving the elimination of fat. However, as
animals on these diets do not attain the compromised

High fat
Owing to the strong links between fatty liver formation
and the metabolic syndrome, animal models have been
developed that imitate western­style, high­fat diets.
Animals are fed, or forcibly fed, a high­fat diet in which
the majority of caloric intake (45–75%) is from fat and/or
variations containing fructose, trans­fats or cholesterol
to induce obesity, insulin resistance and hepatic damage.
Compared with the MCD model, the degree of liver
injury is not as severe (although this is dependent on the
species strain). This can be viewed as advantageous as it
allows researchers working with knockout mice to judge
whether liver injury is aggravated by the high­fat diet.
In a rat model of high­fat diet feeding (71% of energy
from fat, 11% from carbohydrates and 18% from
protein), the resulting histopathology resembled that
seen in human NASH;42 the rats had increased insulin
levels, insulin resistance, hepatic intracellular lipid
accumulation, oxidative stress, collagen type I and α1(I)
procollagen mRNA upregulation, an increase in TNF
levels and abnormal mitochondria.
To increase the ingestion of fat from high­fat diets,
gastric overnutrition has been employed through an
implanted gastrostomy tube. 43 C57BL/6 mice given
a liquid emulsion of 37% of calories from fat (corn
oil) and 39% of calories from dextrose became obese,
had increased levels of visceral white adipose tissue,
demon strated hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemia,
hyperleptinemia, glucose intolerance and insulin resis­
tance and developed steatohepatitis. The effect of a

high­fat diet seems to be more pronounced in rats than
mice as the pathology better resembles that seen in
human NASH.44
A variation of the above model in which rats were
fed high levels of polyunsaturated corn oil via an intra­
gastric cannula caused similar metabolic changes, but
also resulted in decreased adiponectin levels, increased
hepatic triglyceride levels, macrophage infiltration and
apoptosis, and focal necrosis accompanied by increased
serum ALT levels.45 Thus, in rodents, high­fat diets can
replicate the altered metabolic parameters seen in human
fatty liver disease, but the hepatic pathological outcome
is not as severe.
Cholesterol and cholate
Insulin resistance is a key pathophysiological correlate
of the metabolic syndrome. It promotes elevated tri­
glyceride and cholesterol levels and increases the risk of
cardiovascular disease.46 For example, mice with muscle­
specific insulin receptor inactivation develop obesity and
have increased levels of plasma triglycerides, analogous
to insulin­resistant humans (who have an increased risk
of developing fatty liver disease over their lifetime).47,48
Consequently, researchers have used atherogenic diets,
containing cholate and cholesterol, to promote athero­
sclerosis—and the resulting liver damage and fibrosis
—in animals.49,50
In mice, cholesterol and cholate can induce dis­
tinct sets of hepatic inflammatory and collagen gene
expression, respectively.51 Dietary cholesterol is also
an important risk factor for the progression of NAFLD
to NASH 52 as it sensitizes the liver to TNF and Fas­
induced steatohepatitis.53 Matsuzawa et al.54 fed mice

an atherogenic diet containing 1.25% cholesterol and
0.5% cholate and observed the progressive formation of
steatosis, inflammation and fibrosis in a time­dependent
manner over 6–24 weeks. Importantly, hepatocellular
ballooning, a characteristic feature of human NASH,
was present at 24 weeks. The incorporation of 60% fat
(cocoa butter) in the diet accelerated the development
of these histopathological features, with hepatocellular
ballooning becoming present at 12 weeks. In addition,
the increased fat component enhanced the activation of
hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), with prominent α­smooth
muscle actin expression (a marker of activated HSCs)
already present at 6 weeks, and increased oxidative stress
at 24 weeks. Taken together, these data suggest that the
combination of a high­fat, cholesterol and cholate diet
can replicate the pathophysiological findings of human
NASH. However, analysis of the metabolic status of mice
fed this diet revealed that they were systemically more
insulin sensitive, but had attained hepatic insulin resis­
tance.54 Indeed, over the course of the experiment, the
mice lost 9% of their body weight and had smaller fat
pads and lower triglyceride levels compared with con­
trols. Thus, although the atherogenic, high­fat diet does
replicate human pathology, the metabolic status differs.
Further studies are required to address whether altera­
tions in fat composition or the addition of other dietary
factors associated with metabolic status, such as fruc­
tose, can lead to this model attaining the relevant human
metabolic parameters.

animal models of fatty liver disease as it promotes
steatosis, proinflammatory responses and intestinal
bacterial overgrowth.

Fructose
In humans, increased levels of fructose consumption—
primarily in the form of corn syrup in soft drinks—are
associated with NAFLD and fibrosis severity.55,56 Fructose
can promote de novo lipogenesis, the formation of reac­
tive oxygen species, and insulin resistance. Its role in
NAFLD has been meticulously reviewed by Lim and
colleagues.57 In mice, the addition of 30% fructose to
drinking water caused a fourfold increase in the levels of
hepatic triglycerides and a marked increase in steatosis
and weight over 8 weeks.58 The same group found that
fructose promoted intestinal bacterial overgrowth, which
lead to increased endotoxin levels in the portal blood,
activation of Kupffer cells and hepatic inflammation.
The treatment of fructose­fed mice with antibiotics or
the feeding of fructose to endotoxin receptor, Toll­like
receptor 4 (TLR4) knockout mice leads to reduced levels
of steatosis and inflammation,58,59 which suggests that
fructose can promote hepatocellular damage.
with regard to NAFLD, no published animal data
have shown that fructose alone can alter metabolic para­
meters, but biochemically it has been argued that fructose
has potent metabolic attributes and can promote insulin
resistance.57 However, it has been shown that the addi­
tion of trans­fats or high levels of fat to a fructose diet
promotes glucose and insulin insensitivity and fatty liver
formation with no fibrosis.60,61 Moreover, feeding mice
a high­fat diet that contains trans­fats induces greater
steatosis and augments hepatic lipogenic gene expres­
sion more than a high­fat diet alone.62 In summary, these

Genetic models

rabbit models of a high-fat diet
The models discussed above do not always reflect the
clinical and histological features of progressive human
NAFLD. Thus, other work has been conducted in
larger mammals. Ogawa et al.63 fed rabbits a high­fat
diet consisting of 12% corn oil and 0.75% cholesterol
for 9 months and observed human­like NASH features
of fibrosis close to cirrhosis. These animals failed to
become obese but they did demonstrate increases in
levels of fasting glucose, insulin and homeostatic model
assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA­IR).
Thus, in conclusion, a number of dietary animal
models are available and all have distinct advantages and
disadvantages; independent investigators should choose
the model most applicable for their study (Table 1). No
single dietary animal model displays the complete range
of histopathological, metabolic and biochemical changes
associated with progression of NAFLD. It is possible that
animals are more resistant to cycles of feeding (over­
nutrition) and fasting (hibernation); humans, in com­
parison, have lost the genetic memory of such events.
Perhaps these mammals can metabolically manage
high fat loads and consequent liver damage better
than humans.
To better examine the role of specific genes in fatty
liver formation, researchers have used genetic models.
Steatosis is characterized by the accumulation of intra­
hepatic lipid. As clarified by Lim et al.,57 this accumula­
tion of intrahepatic lipid can occur through the following
mechanisms: an increase in the ingestion of calories,
influx of free fatty acids and de novo lipogenesis; or
through a decrease in hepatic β­oxidation of fatty acids
and triglyceride export. Studies have focused on these
mechanisms, and removed or overexpressed genes to
assess their role in fatty liver formation. This area has
been extensively reviewed by others and so only recent
significant examples are considered in this Review.17,34,64,65
The focus here is the inflammatory role of the metabolic
syndrome in NAFLD (Table 2).

Adipocyte-mediated inflammation
Adipose tissue is the body’s largest endocrine organ and
produces an array of biologically active proteins (termed
adipokines)—including leptin, adiponectin, TNF, IL­6
and resistin. Obesity is characterized by chronic low­
grade inflammation caused by the increased secretion
of proinflammatory adipokines and reduced levels of
adiponectin. Concomitantly, there is an increase in the
number and activation status of adipose­infiltrating
macrophages that potentiates further inflammation. 66
Studies have also shown that anti­inflammatory regula­
tory T cells are lost from lean fat and that CD8+ effector
T cells promote macrophage recruitment and adipose

of these factors is to inhibit the activity of the insulin
receptor signaling pathway leading to the development
of insulin resistance and diabetes.69 This finding has led
researchers to investigate the role of adipocytes in fatty
liver formation. The following sections discuss the evi­
dence for crosstalk between adipose tissue and the liver
that is pathogenically associated with the development
of NAFLD.

Tomita et al.75 investigated the role of ADIPOR2 sig­
naling in the MCD model of NASH by injecting mice
with either ADIPOR2 short hairpin RNA­expressing
adenovirus (to suppress ADIPOR2) or ADIPOR2 over­
expressing adenovirus. In these studies, ADIPOR2
expression protected against the development of steato­
hepatitis (steatosis, inflammation, oxidative stress
and fibrosis). These data suggest that adipose­derived
adiponectin protects against NAFLD.

Adiponectin
Adiponectin null mice are more susceptible to the
develop ment of fibrosis induced by carbon tetra­
choloride; supplementation with adiponectin prevents
fibrosis, in part mediated by reduced production of
TGF­β1.70 Adiponectin null mice fed the CDAA diet
develop liver cirrhosis and hepatic tumors, whereas
wild­type mice show only simple steatosis.71 when fed
a high­fat diet containing 60% of the calories from fat,
adiponectin null mice develop fibrosing hepatitis with
clear hepatocyte ballooning, spotty necrosis and peri­
cellular fibrosis.72 Importantly, adiponectin null mice
have increased levels of TNF and IL­6, which suggests
that reduced levels of adiponectin promote inflammation
in tissues, including the liver.73,74
The adiponectin receptor ADIPOR2 is the most
strongly expressed adiponectin receptor in the liver.

Regulation of Wnt signaling
In a differential genetic screen of adipose tissues from
wild­type mice fed either normal chow or a high­fat,
high­sucrose (HF–HS) diet, secreted frizzled­related
protein 5 (SFRP5) was identified as being downregulated
in HF–HS fed mice.76 SFRP5 sequesters wnt signaling
proteins to prevent binding to wnt receptors. In obese
humans, reductions in SFRP5 levels were paralleled
by increases in the levels of TNF and HOMA­IR. The
investigators generated Sfrp5–/– mice and no metabolic

clearance and insulin sensitivity, and increased levels
of triglycerides, inflammation (increased numbers of
macrophages and an increase in the levels of IL­6, TNF
and MCP1) and steatosis compared with wild­type mice

High‑fat‑diet‑promoted adipocyte apoptosis
Genetic studies have shown that reductions in adipo­
cyte apoptosis can reduce liver steatosis. Alkhouri et al.77
observed marked increases in adipocyte apoptosis in diet­
induced obesity in mice. The researchers then studied
Bid null mice fed a high­fat diet. Bid (BH3 interacting
domain death agonist) is a key proapoptotic molecule
and its absence during obesity induced by a high­fat diet
reduces adipocyte apoptosis, adipose tissue inflammation
and macrophage number, and protects against systemic
insulin resistance and steatosis formation.
However, mediators of apoptosis, such as Fas (also
known as CD95), may also regulate inflammatory events.
wueest et al.20 observed that the selective deletion of Fas
from adipocytes alleviated adipose tissue inflamma­
tion and hepatic steatosis in mice. Hyperinsulinemic­
euglycemic clamp studies illustrated that wild­type mice
fed the high­fat diet developed hepatic insulin resistance,
whereas Fas knockout mice fed the high­fat diet were
protected and had reduced circulating levels of free fatty
acids. Fas can also regulate inflammation, and the authors
found reduced adipocyte, IL­6, CD11b, MCP1 and resis­
tin mRNA levels in Fas knockout mice, while levels of
noninflammatory IL­10 and arginase 1 were increased.
Mechanistically, the authors speculated that the elevated
levels of the dominant proinflammatory cytokine IL­6
and free fatty acids (caused by the activation of Fas) could
promote hepatic insulin resistance and steatosis.

Linking adipose inflammation and steatosis
The above studies support the hypothesis that factors
(or the lack of factors) generated by adipose tissue during
obesity can potentiate hepatic inflammation, increase
resistance to insulin and result in production of free fatty
acids and hepatic de novo lipogenesis to cause steatosis.
Given the direct physical links between visceral abdomi­
nal fat and the liver, this concept is plausible. Moreover,
mice that lack IL­6 or TNF receptor 1 (TNFR1) have
reduced levels of hepatic lipid and macrophage and
neutrophil infiltration when fed a high­fat diet, result­
ing in the prevention of steatohepatitis.78 Importantly,
the same study found that IL­6 and TNF receptor sig­
naling enhanced by a high­fat diet promoted HCC in
mice. These data indicate the role of underlying obesity,
inflammation and fatty liver in HCC formation.
Given the involvement of TNF signaling, it has been
shown that NFκB (a downstream target) and its trans­
criptional targets are upregulated in the livers of mice fed
a high­fat diet.79 Moreover, the genetic overexpression
of IκB kinase (IKK­β) led to NFκB activation, increased
glucose levels and hepatic and systemic insulin resistance,
and increased hepatic production of proinflammatory
IL­6, IL­1 and TNF. Although the transgenic mice were

not fed a high­fat diet, these studies indicate that hepatic
inflammation and steatosis are directly linked.
Nevertheless, in the other direction, researchers
have inhibited NFκB signaling and have surprisingly
observed that these mice develop steatohepatitis and
HCC.80 Here, the selective hepatic deletion of NFκB­
essential­modulator (NeMO, or inhibitor of κB kinase γ
[IKBKG]), which mediates the phosphorylation of the
inhibitors of NFκB (IκBs) and their subsequent degrada­
tion, abrogates NFκB activity to make hepatocytes more
sensitive to TNF­induced apoptosis. The enhanced
hepatocyte cell death triggers more inflammation
and hepatocyte regeneration and increases the likeli­
hood of oncogenic mutations and eventual liver cancer
development. The authors found that Nemo–/– hepatocytes
were more sensitive to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) chal­
lenge, suggesting the involvement of innate immunity,
which has been shown by others to be a driver of pro­
gression to steatohepatitis (see below). Mechanistically,
it was observed that hepatic­NeMO­deficient mice fed a
high­fat diet did not demonstrate upregulation of peroxi­
some proliferator­activated receptor (PPAR)­α. This led
to reduced β­oxidation and upregulated levels of PPAR­γ,
sterol regulatory element binding protein (SReBP­1), and
fatty acid synthase to increase de novo lipid synthesis and
macrovesicular steatosis and to increased HCC occur­
rence.81 These data suggest that TNF signaling through
NFκB, mediated by adipocytes on the liver or by the liver
itself, has an important role in fatty liver disease.
Further downstream from TNF­mediated signal­
ing is JNK. Increased JNK activity can promote insulin
resistance, and JNK1–/– mice have decreased adiposity,
improved insulin sensitivity and enhanced insulin recep­
tor signaling during obesity.82 This suggests a role for
JNK in steatosis. Indeed, JNK1–/– mice fed the MCD diet,
which promotes hepatic oxidative stress and can induce
JNK1 activity, have significantly reduced steatohepatitis
compared with wild­type mice fed the MCD diet. 37
Mechanistically, studies have shown that JNK1–/– mice
have less hepatic inflammation and fibrosis, but similar
levels of steatosis compared with wild­type mice when
fed the CDAA diet. Significantly, the authors elegantly
showed that the attenuated inflammation and fibrosis
in JNK1–/– mice is due to hematopoietic cells, since wild­
type mice transplanted with bone marrow cells from
JNK1–/– mice had reduced inflammation and fibrosis
when compared with the wild­type.
In summary, NAFLD can be promoted by inflamma­
tory signals generated by a variety of cellular sources,
including adipose tissue. The net affect of these pro­
inflammatory signals is to act on the liver to generate
further hepatic inflammation and steatosis (Figure 3).

Additional causes of fatty liver
it is not just the fat
The impression from the above studies is that inflamma­
tion in the liver and in tissues other than the liver (for
example, adipose tissue) can be a driving force for steat­
osis formation. Nevertheless, reports suggest that there are
other mechanisms at play and these are discussed below.

Cholesterol
The ‘two­hit’ model purports that hepatic steatosis
is the first hit and a requirement for further liver injury.
New reports have questioned this concept. For example,
a hyperlipidemic ‘humanized’ Apoe2 (apolipoprotein e)
knock­in mouse fed a western­style, high­fat diet (con­
taining 21% fat and 0.2% cholesterol) developed steatosis,
inflammation and early fibrosis after just 4 days. APOe2
has a greatly reduced affinity for the LDL receptor, so
Apoe2 knock­in mice have a plasma lipoprotein profile
that resembles human type III hyperlipoproteinemia
(which is characterized by increased levels of plasma
chole sterol and triglycerides owing to the impaired
clearance of chylomicron and VLDL remnants).83 In
these knock­in mice, APOe2 was highly expressed by
macrophages and it was observed that after just 2 days
an increased number of liver CD68+ cells, represent­
ing Kupffer cells and macrophages, preceded steatosis
formation. In a further study the investigators observed
that the cells were bloated, foamy Kupffer cells. Omitting
cholesterol from the diet greatly reduced hepatic foam
cell formation and prevented the onset of inflammation,
without affecting steatosis.52
In a subsequent study, the same investigators tested the
concept that although these mice are hyperlipidemic,
the lipoproteins have a lengthened serum circulating time
and are more likely to undergo modification and scav­
enging by Kupffer cells, resulting in Kupffer cell activa­
tion and subsequent liver inflammation and foam cell
formation.84 Kupffer cells take up modified lipoproteins
through scavenger receptors such as macrophage scaven­
ger receptor 1 (MSR1; acetylated low­density lipoprotein)
and CD36. The authors transplanted bone marrow from
wild­type or Msr1–/– and Cd36–/– mice into lethally irradi­
ated, LDL­receptor­knockout (Lldr–/–) mice fed a high­
fat (21% butter), 0.2% cholesterol diet. The absence of
Msr1 and Cd36 greatly reduced hepatic inflammation,
apoptosis, lipid oxidation and fibrosis, but had no affect
on steatosis formation. Interestingly, however, the foam
cell size and cholesterol content in Msr1+/+Cd36+/+ and
Msr1–/–Cd36–/– transplanted mice was the same, suggest­
ing that hepatic inflammation mediated through MSR1
and CD36 is independent of foam cell formation.
In a similar but separate study, cholesteryl ester
hydrolase (CeH), which catalyzes the hydrolysis of
intracellular stored cholesteryl esters to increase their
cellular removal, was specifically overexpressed in the
macrophages of Ldlr–/– mice.85 Transgenic Ldlr–/– CeH
mice fed a high­fat diet had improved insulin sensitiv­
ity and reduced levels of the proinflammatory cytokines
IL­1β, IL­6 and MCP1, and reduced migration of macro­
phages into adipose tissues. In a similar setting, mice
with transgenic overexpression of hepatic cholesterol
7α­hydroxylase (which converts cholesterol into bile
acids) demonstrated improved insulin sensitivity and
glucose utilization, preventing fatty liver formation.86
Taken together, the use of these genetic and high­fat diet
experimental models show that cholesterol is important
in promoting hepatic and systemic inflammation, in
governing insulin and glucose tolerance, and that the

innate immunity
The liver is constantly exposed to microbial flora from
gut bacteria that are carried to the liver via the portal
circulation. In the healthy liver, immune tolerance to
these constituents is active. However, in the diseased liver
or where there is the introduction of new or abundant
bacterial products, the state of tolerance is lost. TLRs
recognize these bacterial products and activate interferon
(IFN)­α/β, NFκB and activator protein 1 (AP1) pro­
inflammatory responses.87 As explained above, a fructose
diet promotes intestinal bacterial overgrowth, increases
LPS levels and involves TLR4, leading to aggravation
of hepatic inflammation. Studies have also shown that
TLR9 is involved in steatohepatitis.88 TLR9 is a receptor
for unmethylated cytosine phosphate guanine­containing

steatotic polymorphisms and mouse models
Studies have suggested that single­nucleotide poly­
morphisms are associated with hepatic steatosis. ethnic
groups such as Asian Indian males have a high preva­
lence of NAFLD and insulin resistance.90 A genome­wide
screen found that a single variant of the gene encoding
the enzyme patatin­like phospholipase domain con­
taining protein 3 (PNPLA3; missense mutation result­
ing in isoleucine to methionine substitution at residue
148 [I148M]) was associated with increased hepatic fat
content independent of BMI and insulin resistance.91
Overexpression of Pnpla3‑I148M in cells and mice pro­
moted the accumulation of triglycerides via disrupted
hydrolysis.92 These finding support the role of mutant
PNPLA3 in promoting hepatic steatosis. Unexpectedly,
however, Pnpla3 –/– mice fed a high­fat diet did not
develop steatosis, but another family protein, PNPLA5,
was shown to compensate for PNPLA3 in muscle,
which suggests redundancy and tissue crosstalk, or that
Pnpla3‑I148M is a gain­of­function mutation.93,94 Using
a similar population group, Petersen et al.95 showed that
polymorphisms in the gene encoding plasma apolipo­
protein C3 (APO3C) are associated with NAFLD and
insulin resistance. Carriers of APO3C variant alleles
had increased levels of fasting plasma APOC3 and tri­
glycerides and reduced triglyceride clearance. Mice that
overexpress APOC3 have hypertriglceridemia and aggra­
vated diet­induced obesity; however, an examination of
liver pathology has not been undertaken.96,97 Thus, in

Conclusions

This Review has explored some of the advantages and
disadvantages of the current range of animal models used
to investigate human NAFLD (Table 1). we have also
presented some of the mouse models of inflammation
that show links with other organs and nonhepatic cell
types on steatosis formation (Table 2). This is concordant
with human data showing that progressive increases in
intrahepatic triglycerides are associated with the gradual
reduction of insulin sensitivity in the liver, skeletal
muscle and adipose tissues of nondiabetic, obese indivi­
duals.98 Similarly, a mouse model has shown that the
action of insulin on the central nervous system (CNS)
can promote adipocyte lipogenesis and the activation of
hepatic IL­6, and highlights that there are probable links
between the CNS and steatosis development that have
not yet been researched. Overall, the studies presented
in this Review favor a model of steatosis development in
which a combination of multiple factors contributes
to human fatty liver formation (Figure 2). The vast
majority of these factors can induce systemic metabolic
changes, steatosis, hepatic inflammation and fibrosis.
Therefore, steatosis should be regarded as part of the
hepatic response to these changes and an integrated
response to the underlying disease process. The factors
that potentiate the transition from simple steatosis to
NASH, some of which we have discussed, should be the
focus of future therapeutic strategies.
Review criteria
Using PubMed and the substrate key terms “fatty liver”,
“NAFLD” or “NASH”, combined with the effector terms
“inflammation”, “steatosis”, “high fat diet”, “insulin
resistance”, “metabolic syndrome”, “cholesterol”,
“innate immunity” and “polymorphisms”, a review of
the literature published from 2005 was conducted.
Mechanistic studies in animals that addressed the
substrate and effector terms were included.
